extracted.intended_audience: general US news readers interested in business, politics, and culture
extracted.subtask_description: A news report describing a corporation's public comments on a controversial social issue and the ensuing political, public, and business reactions. Focuses on company statements, protests, municipal responses, consumer actions, and likely business impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate treatment standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chick-fil-A culture and service tradition is to treat every person with honor, dignity and respect — regardless of their belief, race, creed, sexual orientation or gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the company's stated policy used to defend itself; the statement emphasizes consistent treatment across its independently run restaurants. The article notes the statement 'has done little to quiet the uproar,' showing that asserting this standard may not be sufficient to calm critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate neutrality on political debates
rubrics_metrics.description: The company said it would stay out of political debates in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a PR response to controversy. Guidance implied: publicly committing to refrain from political advocacy is a potential strategy to reduce backlash after leadership comments generate protest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-advocacy / respect for rights criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Public officials said they did not welcome an individual or business that will 'continue to advocate against people's rights' or promote intolerance; such advocacy makes a company unwelcome in their city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes from Boston and Philadelphia officials frame municipal acceptance as contingent on whether a company's leaders advocate against citizens' rights. This standard is used to justify blocking or discouraging restaurant openings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with local values standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Local leaders asserted that 'Chick-fil-A's values are not Chicago values' and that corporate values should be respectful of residents, neighbors and family members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by city leaders to evaluate whether a company fits community norms; can be invoked to oppose expansion even when objections are framed as cultural rather than legal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer-response as reputational metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Public reaction (boycotts, appreciation days, protests, social media posts) is a key metric for measuring reputational fallout and potential business impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents calls for boycotts, a proposed 'Chick-fil-A Appreciation Day' with hundreds of thousands on Facebook, GLAAD's National Same-Sex Kiss Day, and protests at openings — all presented as measurable consumer/political responses that can influence brand perception and sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-discrimination by service as defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Supporters argue the company has 'done nothing wrong' because it is not banning anyone from restaurants or refusing to serve patrons despite its leadership's statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an articulated defense used to distinguish private speech from discriminatory business practice. The article presents it as a reason some customers see no wrongdoing and continue patronizing the chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business-impact uncertainty metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term impact on the company's bottom line depends on whether consumers 'vote with their wallet'; a business expert expects the impact to be 'fairly marginal' but acknowledges uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: analysts view short-term protests as unlikely to cause major financial damage but note that sustained consumer action could produce measurable effects. The article cites an expert saying it's difficult to predict how large the impact will be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion context as explanatory criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifts in public attitudes (polling showing majority support for same-sex marriage, increases in people who know someone gay, changes in beliefs about changing sexual orientation) provide context for why reactions are strong and politically consequential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses polling and trend data to explain the social backdrop that shapes reactions. This implies that evaluating corporate comments requires situating them against contemporary public-opinion metrics.
